scenario: AITA for telling someone disabled they should leave the gym | Throwaway for the usual reasons I go to the gym a few times a week as it's something I enjoy. Yesterday I was there for the first time this year and there was lots of new people which is to be expected this time of year with people making resolutions they can't stick to. Anyway I was minding my own business when I looked up and saw an overweight woman come in who had a walking stick, she also had who turned out to be her husband with her who looked like a gym regular. I saw her get on the exercise bike for about 20 minutes then she moved to the weight machines. Because of her disability she couldn't manage on and off the machines herself and her husband was helping her on and off between his workout. I was concerned about this and no staff were about so I went upto her and told her I think it's for the best she leaves the gym as she's clearly not able bodied enough for it (looking back now I should have worded it better). Her husband then came up and asked if everything was ok and I told him my concerns. He raised his voice slightly at me and told me to mind my own business as he's qualified in training different sports and she was in safe hands. I then told them I don't think the gym management would be too happy at someone disabled and unable to get on and off the machines being in the gym. He told me his wife wasn't actually allowed to join the gym without a Dr's letter and also a meeting with the gym manager to come up with a plan for her to safety evacuate the building with the help of staff and all staff were aware of her problems. At this point I realised they weren't going to leave so went back to my workout. Today I told my friend what happened and he told me I'm an idiot who should learn to mind his own business or try encourage someone who's new to the gym. He doesn't attend the gym so I don't feel he understands the kind of environment she was in. He also seems to think my membership could be at risk for what I said

Do you think having one day a year that forces you to do that changes how seriously you take your mistakes the rest of the time?

What a profound and introspective question. Having a day like Yom Kippur, dedicated to reflection, atonement, and self-improvement, can indeed have a significant impact on how one approaches mistakes and personal growth throughout the year. By setting aside a specific day to confront and acknowledge past mistakes, individuals can develop a greater sense of accountability and responsibility for their actions. This intentional reflection can lead to a deeper understanding of the consequences of their mistakes and a stronger motivation to make amends and change their behavior. Having a dedicated day for introspection can also help individuals develop a greater sense of self-awareness, which can, in turn, influence their decision-making and behavior throughout the year. By regularly examining their actions and their impact on others, individuals may become more mindful of the potential consequences of their choices and more inclined to consider the well-being of those around them. Moreover, the annual practice of Yom Kippur can foster a sense of humility and recognition of one's own fallibility. This can lead to a greater willingness to apologize, make amends, and learn from mistakes, rather than trying to justify or deny them. By acknowledging and accepting their mistakes, individuals can develop a more growth-oriented mindset, which can help them approach challenges and setbacks with a greater sense of resilience and determination. It's also worth noting that the act of seeking forgiveness and making amends can have a profound impact on relationships and personal growth. By taking responsibility for past wrongs and working to repair harm, individuals can strengthen their connections with others, rebuild trust, and develop a greater sense of empathy and compassion. Overall, having a day like Yom Kippur can indeed change how seriously one takes their mistakes and can have a lasting impact on personal growth, relationships, and overall well-being. By incorporating regular reflection, self-awareness, and a willingness to learn from mistakes, individuals can cultivate a more mindful, compassionate, and responsible approach to life.
